slides.title: Disk Scheduling Basics
content: Disk scheduling is the process by which the operating system decides the order of servicing disk I/O requests to minimize seek time and improve performance
Key metrics include seek time, rotational latency, throughput, and response time
Efficient scheduling reduces disk head movement and improves overall system performance
It ensures fairness and prevents indefinite delays in servicing requests

slides.title: Disk Scheduling Algorithms
content: FCFS serves requests in arrival order and is simple but inefficient for seek time optimization
SSTF selects the closest request to minimize seek time but may cause starvation
SCAN moves the disk head in one direction servicing requests and then reverses direction
C-SCAN provides uniform wait time by scanning in one direction and jumping back to start
LOOK and C-LOOK optimize SCAN by avoiding unnecessary movement beyond last request :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

slides.title: RAID (Disk Management)
content: RAID combines multiple physical disks into a single logical unit to improve performance and reliability :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
Striping improves speed by distributing data across disks while mirroring provides redundancy
RAID 0 offers high performance without fault tolerance, RAID 1 provides full redundancy
RAID 5 and RAID 6 use parity for fault tolerance, while RAID 10 combines performance and reliability

slides.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
content: IPC enables processes to communicate and synchronize using mechanisms like message passing and shared memory :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
Message passing uses send and receive operations for communication without shared memory
Shared memory allows processes to directly access common memory for faster communication
Synchronization mechanisms like semaphores ensure safe data sharing between processes

slides.title: Signals & Signal Handling
content: A signal is a software interrupt used by the OS to notify a process about events like errors or external actions :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
Signals can be generated by user input, system events, or other processes
Processes can handle signals using default actions or custom signal handlers
Common signals include SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGKILL, and SIGSEGV for process control

slides.title: Overall Importance
content: Disk scheduling improves performance by reducing access time and optimizing disk operations
RAID enhances data reliability and system availability through redundancy
IPC enables efficient communication between processes in multitasking environments
Signals provide quick communication for handling events and process control in operating systems
